analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering doctor, hospital, dental, and nursing care, funded by a new tax on transactions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in January 2003, sent to their health subcommittees, and never received a hearing or vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up a national health insurance program run by a new federal board, working through state and local agencies. Everyone who met a work-history requirement, plus their dependents, would be covered for medical, dental, hospital, home-nursing, and related services, with free choice of doctor and hospital. The program would be paid for by a new value-added tax — a tax added at each stage of producing and selling goods and services — deposited into a dedicated trust fund. Medicare beneficiaries would keep Medicare and get only the extra services this program covers.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people and their dependents who meet the wage-history requirements, especially the uninsured and underinsured who today face 'shattering' costs for serious illness; the bill's stated purpose is prepaid health insurance on a social-insurance principle, with no discrimination by race, creed, or color and free choice of physician [S3]. Providers who sign agreements get fee-for-service, per-capita, or salary payment, and hospitals are paid reasonable costs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services (lab work, X-rays, expensive drugs, eyeglasses) available as benefits to eligible individuals [S2] [S3].
Guarantees every eligible person free choice of physician, dentist, hospital, and other providers, with the right to change providers [S2] [S3].

Covers anyone with a qualifying work record ($2,000 in wages in four of the last six quarters, or a similar longer-period test), plus Social Security and civil-service beneficiaries and their dependents; needy people not otherwise eligible can be covered through reimbursement agreements with public agencies [S3].

Prohibits discrimination on account of race, creed, or color in both receiving services and participating as a provider, and keeps individual health information confidential with criminal penalties for disclosure [S3].
Funds the program through a dedicated National Health Care Trust Fund filled by a new value-added tax, so the money can be used only for this program [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who buys goods and services, through the new value-added tax imposed on commercial transactions (with the rate set at zero for specified transactions); private health insurers would lose most of their role, and providers would be paid under public fee schedules and hospital cost limits instead of private negotiated rates [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers via a new VAT; insurers

drawbacks.text: The financing is a value-added tax on sales of property and services, a tax economists widely recognize as regressive — it takes a larger share of income from lower-income households than from wealthier ones [S2] [S3].

Coverage is tied to a work record: a person must have earned at least $2,000 in wages in four of the last six quarters (or meet similar tests) to qualify, so people with little or no covered earnings are not eligible on their own, though public agencies can pay for their care [S3].

The board may limit dental, home-nursing, or auxiliary services if personnel, facilities, or funds are inadequate, and hospital stays are capped at 60 days a year, with mental-hospital coverage excluded [S2] [S3].
Medicare beneficiaries get nothing beyond what Medicare already pays — the program only fills Medicare's gaps, so the two systems run side by side rather than being merged [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would guarantee universal (work-linked) coverage with free choice of provider and no premiums or deductibles, paid from a dedicated tax — a large gain for ordinary families facing medical bills. The cost side is real: the value-added tax would fall proportionally hardest on lower-income households, and the program starts with service limits (60 hospital days, possible restrictions on dental and auxiliary care) until funding and capacity catch up. It also leaves Medicare separate instead of merging it, creating two parallel systems. On balance it is a major benefit to ordinary people, with the tax design as its weakest feature.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 7, 2003 and sent to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, which passed it to their health subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Rep. John D. Dingell (D-MI) introduced the National Health Insurance Act on January 7, 2003, as the first bill of the 108th Congress [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, and on January 23 and February 3, 2003, respectively, each committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action in either chamber before the 108th Congress ended [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and the existing employer-based insurance system, which would have lost most of their role under a national program; no one began paying the new value-added tax either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the sole sponsor was a Democrat and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, while the committees that buried it were chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: A national program paying providers directly out of a public trust fund would replace most private health coverage, eliminating the industry's core role. Insurers keep only a marginal role through optional agreements with state agencies [S3].
The program covers unusually expensive prescribed drugs as a benefit, and a single public purchaser would pay less than fragmented private payers. Cheaper drugs are a direct gain for patients [S3].
Hospitals gain a universal payer with no uninsured patients, but must accept payment at reasonable cost with board-set maximum rates and the least expensive adequate accommodations [S3].

Doctors keep free choice of practice locale, the right to reject patients, and a choice of fee-for-service, per-capita, or salary payment, but at public fee schedules rather than private rates. Participation is voluntary [S3].
